title: Scuffling Toronto Blue Jays see Daulton Varsho (left knee) exit after 3 innings
content:
PHOENIX — In the latest hit to the Toronto Blue Jays’ scuffling and injury-depleted lineup, outfielder Daulton Varsho was removed in the third inning of Friday’s game against the Arizona Diamondbacks due to left knee discomfort. The outfielder is day to day, manager John Schneider said postgame.

With four key bats already on the injured list, losing Varsho, even for a brief period, will put more strain on Toronto’s lineup.

Varsho swung at two pitches in his first-inning at-bat, showing no signs of discomfort after either. He played two balls in the bottom of the second, corralling a line drive and fielding a single. Those defensive plays were his last before leaving Friday’s contest.

Varsho, Schneider said, informed the team before the game of discomfort in his knee and lower quad. The Jays elected to remove him in the third to “be extra careful,” Schneider said.

The Jays, who lost Anthony Santander to shoulder surgery ahead of spring training, have since placed George Springer (toe), Addison Barger (ankles) and Alejandro Kirk (thumb) on the IL. Barger and Springer won’t likely be out long term but are still at least a week away from rejoining the club.

By Steamer wRC+ projections, Springer, Kirk and Barger represented three of Toronto’s five best offensive players. Varsho, who shifted to the second spot in Toronto’s lineup after the injuries, has been one of the team’s few performing players lately. In his last six games before Friday’s contest, the outfielder hit three homers with a 1.215 OPS.

For a Jays team that hasn’t won a series since Opening Day weekend, it can’t afford many more injuries. Vladimir Guerrero Jr., too, was checked out by Toronto’s medical staff in the eighth inning after clipping his left index finger on an opponent’s jersey, but he stayed in the game. He, Schneider said, should be fine to play Saturday.

The Jays have the backups needed to cover a day for Guerrero or Varsho, if needed. They have prospects in Triple A to call up and bench players to slide into the starting lineup. Still, the Jays can’t afford to lose many more key players.
